nameStory: Torrey's wild licorice gets its sweet name from a delightful surprise—if you chew on its leaves or roots, you'll taste something remarkably similar to black licorice candy! The plant was named after John Torrey, a famous 19th-century American botanist who helped catalog many of our native plants. It's called 'wild' licorice because it's completely unrelated to the true licorice plant that flavors candy—nature just happened to create the same taste twice!
description: Torrey's wild licorice is a low-growing woodland plant that spreads along the forest floor like a green carpet. It's a member of the bedstraw family, with delicate square stems and small leaves arranged in neat whorls (circles) around the stem. The plant rarely gets taller than 8-12 inches and produces tiny, inconspicuous flowers. What makes it special isn't its looks—it's that unmistakable licorice flavor that surprises anyone who gives it a taste.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls of 4-6 around square stems, with three prominent parallel veins running lengthwise that you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant that spreads horizontally along the ground, forming loose mats in shaded woodland areas

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or greenish flowers so small they're easy to miss, appearing in sparse clusters along the stem in summer

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly square stems that feel smooth to the touch, unlike the sticky or rough stems of many other bedstraws

idTips.label: Taste
idTips.description: Leaves and roots have a distinct sweet licorice flavor when chewed—a unique identifying feature among New England plants

habitat: Look for Torrey's wild licorice in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with deep leaf litter. It thrives in the dappled shade under maple, oak, and beech trees, often growing alongside other woodland wildflowers like trilliums and wild ginger. You'll most commonly find it on gentle slopes and in valley bottoms where the soil stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the forest floor warms, with fresh green whorls of leaves unfurling along last year's stems. This is when the licorice flavor is most pronounced.
seasonality.summer: Tiny flowers bloom inconspicuously while the plant reaches its full spreading growth. The distinctive three-veined leaves are easiest to identify now.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may yellow slightly but often stay green well into autumn. Small fruits develop but are rarely noticed among the fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, leaving only underground rhizomes. Look for dried square stems poking through snow as identification clues.

funFact: This plant is like nature's own candy factory—it produces the exact same chemical compound (glycyrrhizin) that gives commercial licorice its flavor, even though it's completely unrelated to the Mediterranean licorice plant used in candy making!
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with other bedstraws, but most have rough or sticky stems while Torrey's feels smooth. The foolproof test? Give it a taste—no other bedstraw in New England has that distinctive licorice flavor. Remember: 'When in doubt, taste it out' (though only after you're confident it's a bedstraw!).
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the licorice flavor, this plant is completely unrelated to true licorice (Glycyrrhiza species) from the Mediterranean. It's a perfect example of convergent evolution—two unrelated plants developing the same chemical compound independently. The bedstraw family also gave us coffee, so you're looking at a distant coffee relative!
compareHints: Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste. While fragrant bedstraw also has three-veined leaves, it smells like vanilla when crushed rather than tasting like licorice. The lance-shaped leaves with prominent parallel veins also set it apart from most other bedstraws which have narrower, less prominently veined leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit.

Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles.
Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern.
Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms.
Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw).
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.

White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips.
